title: Touhou: Grand Gensokyo Adventure
storyOverview:
You are a human in Gensokyo — either an outsider who just got spirited away through a void full of staring eyes, or a native scraping by in the Human Village with a rumbling stomach and a little self-defense training. Either way, the situation is the same: you are soft, edible, and surrounded by beings who could vaporize you by accident.

THE WORLD: Gensokyo is a pocket of old Japan sealed behind the Hakurei Barrier since 1885 — the place where forgotten gods, youkai, vampires, ghosts, and other things humanity stopped believing in went to keep existing. It is gorgeous. It is whimsical. It will absolutely eat you. Civilization means the Human Village: markets, shrines, Keine Kamishirasawa's temple school, gossip, odd jobs, and walls that youkai politely respect during business hours. Beyond it sprawls everything else — the mushroom-choked Forest of Magic, the Bamboo Forest of the Lost, the Misty Lake and the Scarlet Devil Mansion on its shore, the kappa workshops of Youkai Mountain, the corpse-flowers of Muenzuka, and the Hakurei Shrine perched on the barrier's edge, where a chronically underpaid shrine maiden keeps the whole mad terrarium in balance.

THE RULES: Open violence between humans and youkai was replaced generations ago by the spell card rules — formalized, nonlethal danmaku duels, curtains of beautiful bullets where declaring your spell card is law and losing means humiliation, not death. It's how disputes get settled, how incidents get resolved, and how a nobody can legally slap a vampire. But the rules only protect you where the rules are watched. In the dark woods, on the old roads, at night — plenty of wild youkai still consider 'human' a food group, and no referee is coming. You can start at zero: no magic, no flight, no spell cards. Danmaku can be learned — through training, through duels, through nearly dying — and every spell card you earn is a name you can throw in something's face.

THE PEOPLE: Reimu Hakurei, the deadpan, donation-starved shrine maiden who solves incidents with extreme prejudice and minimal enthusiasm. Marisa Kirisame, the human magician who 'borrows' everything not nailed down and will happily deputize you into her heists. Rumia, the giggling darkness youkai who smells humans on the wind. Keine, half-beast schoolteacher and the village's fierce protector, who might reluctantly train you. Cirno, self-declared strongest ice fairy. Mystia, whose night-song blinds travelers so she can sing them to her grilled lamprey stand — or worse. The Scarlet Devil Mansion crew: the vampire Remilia and her impeccable, knife-happy maid Sakuya. Eientei in the bamboo, with its moon doctor Eirin and the immortal firebrand Mokou. Yukari Yakumo, the gap youkai who opens holes in reality and finds you interesting, which is not a compliment. And Seija Kijin, the amanojaku who despises everyone Gensokyo loves — the worse your reputation gets, the sweeter she'll treat you.

YOUR STORY: Word travels in Gensokyo. Save a farmer from a youkai, solve an incident, cheat a tengu reporter — the village will coin you a title and it will stick. Build fame or infamy; be a saint in public and a bastard in the dark; hoard yen, spell cards, and strange artifacts. Incidents erupt regularly — mists blot the sun, seasons break, the moon gets stolen — and nobodies who get involved stop being nobodies fast.

TONE: Sunlit fairy-tale whimsy stretched over real teeth. Fairies swear like sailors, monsters are charming right up until they aren't, danmaku is beautiful and duels are survivable — but the wilderness at night is not a duel. Comedy, menace, and wonder in the same breath.

TAGS: fantasy, open world, adventure, anime, action, comedy
storySoFar:
Gensokyo: a sealed land of forgotten gods and hungry youkai, hidden behind the Hakurei Barrier since 1885. Here, humans are precious and humans are prey — often to the same creature, depending on the hour and the paperwork. Formal danmaku duels under the spell card rules keep the peace where anyone's watching; the dark roads and deep forests are another matter. You are human, unremarkable, and very much on the menu. But danmaku can be learned, reputations can be built, and in Gensokyo, nobodies who survive their first week have a way of becoming legends. Or dinner.

---

You wake in the middle of the night because the air in your room has changed — and because there is a hole in it. A seam of darkness hangs above the floor, edges tied with red ribbons, and the darkness inside is full of eyes, all of them looking at you. A woman leans out of the gap like a neighbor over a fence: golden eyes, a parasol indoors, a smile with entirely too much geometry behind it.

"Don't scream, it's rude," says Yukari Yakumo pleasantly. "I've been watching you. Don't make that face — I watch everyone, you're just recently interesting. Something is about to go wrong in Gensokyo. Something delicious. And I find it so much more entertaining when a little human is standing in exactly the right spot when it does." She extends a white-gloved hand through the gap. "I'll even pay. Or I can close this hole and you can go back to sleep and be nobody. Choose quickly — I get bored."

SUMMARY^1: The story introduces the dangerous world of Gensokyo, where humans are prey and conflicts are settled via non-lethal danmaku duels. The protagonist is approached in their room by Yukari Yakumo, a powerful gap youkai, who offers them the chance to move beyond their unremarkable status by involving themselves in a mysterious upcoming incident.

> I decide to take the hand, but only after negotiating a generous advance to buy a proper blade and supplies.

Yukari’s smile widens, her eyes glinting with a mixture of amusement and genuine curiosity. She doesn't seem offended by your audacity; in fact, the fact that you're haggling with a gap youkai while still in your pajamas seems to earn you a flicker of respect. "A negotiator! How refreshing. Most of your kind just stutter or faint," she purrs, her gloved hand remaining outstretched. With a flick of her wrist, a small, ornate pouch of heavy gold coins and a few crisp, high-denomination bills materialize out of a miniature rift and land with a satisfying *thud* on your bedside table. It is more money than most villagers see in a year. "Consider it a down payment on your curiosity. Now, take my hand before I decide you're too greedy to be fun." As you grip her fingers, the world tilts violently. The walls of your room don't just vanish; they fold inward like origami, and you are yanked through a freezing, kaleidoscopic void of staring eyes and floating fragments of architecture before being spat out onto a dirt path under a sky of bruised purple and gold.

SUMMARY^1: After negotiating a payment, the protagonist accepts Yukari's offer. Yukari provides a generous sum of money and pulls the protagonist through a gap in reality, transporting them to a mysterious location under a twilight sky.

You land hard on your backside, the air knocking out of you as you find yourself on the outskirts of the Human Village. The scent of woodsmoke and grilled lamprey wafts through the air, but there is an unsettling stillness to the night. The gold pouch is still clutched in your hand, but your lack of equipment is immediately apparent. You are standing near a weathered signpost that points toward the village center and the Forest of Magic. The path is dimly lit by a few flickering stone lanterns, and the silence is periodically broken by the distant, haunting call of a bird that sounds far too much like a laughing child.

> I decide to scavenge the village outskirts for a dark cloak and sturdy boots before seeking a spyglass.

SUMMARY^1: The protagonist arrives on the outskirts of the Human Village, where they find themselves poorly equipped despite their newfound wealth. Amidst an eerie, silent atmosphere, the protagonist decides to prioritize acquiring basic gear, such as a cloak and boots, and a spyglass.

You spend the next hour scouring the outskirts of the village, moving through the long shadows cast by the eaves of warehouses and storage sheds. Luck favors the bold—or the well-funded—as you find a sturdy pair of leather boots and a heavy, charcoal-colored travel cloak left in a drying rack behind a tanner's workshop; the owner seems unlikely to miss them in the dead of night, and the coins in your pocket make it easy to "acquire" a few more necessities from an unattended laundry line. Once dressed for the elements, you make your way toward the village center, navigating the narrow, winding alleys. You find a small, cluttered curiosity shop that remains partially open for late-night travelers, its windows glowing with a dim, amber light. The proprietor, a frail man with thick spectacles, doesn't even look up from his ledger as you browse the shelves of occult trinkets and navigational tools. After a bit of digging through a bin of salvaged maritime gear, you locate a brass spyglass—slightly tarnished but with a lens that remains clear and sharp. You pay the man in gold, the heavy coins clinking loudly on the wooden counter, and step back out into the night, now equipped and inconspicuous.

> I decide to scour the curiosity shop for a light crossbow and a versatile survival knife with a built-in flint.

SUMMARY^1: The protagonist acquires a cloak and boots from the village outskirts and visits a late-night curiosity shop. After purchasing a brass spyglass, they decide to search the shop further for a light crossbow and a survival knife to complete their equipment.

SUMMARY^2: Yukari Yakumo recruits the protagonist into her schemes, offering payment for their involvement in an upcoming incident. After being transported to the outskirts of the Human Village via a gap in reality, the protagonist focuses on survival by purchasing essential gear. They acquire a cloak, boots, and a brass spyglass from a curiosity shop, and intend to find weapons to protect themselves in the wilderness.

You turn back into the amber glow of the curiosity shop, your eyes scanning the cluttered walls for something with a bit more bite than a spyglass. The proprietor, still hunched over his ledger, sighs as the door chimes again, finally glancing up with a weary, bloodshot gaze. He doesn't ask what you're looking for; he simply points a bony finger toward a dusty corner where a collection of "practicals" is kept. There, resting on a velvet tray that has seen better decades, is a compact, blackened-steel light crossbow with a folding limb—perfect for concealment and quick deployment. Beside it lies a heavy-duty survival knife, its blade matte-grey and thick enough to chop through thicket or bone, with a sturdy flint-striker integrated into the pommel of the hilt. You lay a few more of Yukari's gold coins on the counter; the man's eyes widen slightly at the purity of the metal, and he quickly wraps the weapons in oilcloth, sliding them across the counter with a hushed, "Hope you're not planning on going toward the forest tonight, traveler. The air's been... thick lately."

"Thick how?" you ask, checking the tension of the crossbow string. The man doesn't look you in the eye, instead focusing on the coins he's now meticulously counting. "Just thick. The kind of night where the shadows move even when the lanterns don't. If you've got a steady hand, you'll do fine. If not, well, the crows are always hungry." He gives a thin, mirthless smile and gestures toward the door, effectively ending the conversation. You step back out into the cool night air, the weight of the steel against your hip providing a sudden, grounding sense of security. For the first time since waking up, you feel less like a guest and more like a combatant.

SUMMARY^1: The protagonist purchases a folding crossbow and a survival knife from the shop. The proprietor warns them about the dangerous, "thick" atmosphere of the night, particularly in the forest, implying a rise in youkai activity. Now armed and equipped, the protagonist feels a newfound sense of security as they prepare to face the dangers of Gensokyo.

> I decide to seek out a portable cooking kit and a waterproof tarp to establish a hidden base of operations.

You double back into the shop, the bell chiming a second time as you scan the cluttered inventory for camping gear. The proprietor lets out a long, rattling sigh, but the sight of more gold coins on the counter quickly erases his irritation. He reaches beneath a heavy oak table and hauls out a compact, cast-iron cooking set—a small pot, a frying pan, and a folding grate—all packed into a canvas roll. Beside it, he produces a heavy-duty, waxed-canvas tarp, waterproof and olive-drab, designed to withstand the torrential rains of the mountains. As you strap the gear to your person, the weight of the pack pulling at your shoulders, you feel a sense of practical readiness. You are no longer just a wanderer in pajamas; you are a prepared operative, stocked with the means to survive the wild and the tools to fight back.

> I decide to look for a reinforced waterproof rucksack to ensure my supplies remain secure and silent while moving through the brush.

SUMMARY^1: The protagonist returns to the shop to purchase a cast-iron cooking kit and a waterproof canvas tarp to prepare for a wilderness camp. By equipping these survival essentials and supplementing them with gold, they transition from a vulnerable outsider into a prepared traveler, though they still seek a reinforced rucksack to keep their gear secure and quiet.

You return to the shop for the final piece of your kit. The proprietor doesn't even wait for you to speak this time; he simply reaches behind a stack of old maps and pulls out a reinforced, waxed-canvas rucksack with heavy leather straps and muted brass buckles. It is designed for silence and endurance, the fabric stiff and water-resistant. As you transfer your gear—the crossbow, the knife, the cooking kit, and the tarp—into the pack, the weight settles comfortably against your spine, and the buckles snap shut with a muffled, professional click. You pay him with a final glint of gold, and the man finally looks at you with a flicker of genuine curiosity, wondering what kind of fool or genius prepares for a wilderness excursion in the middle of a moonlit night. You step out of the shop and onto the dirt path, your silhouette now broadened by the pack, your footsteps dampened by the sturdy boots, and your supplies secured against the dampness of the Gensokyo night.

> I decide to purchase several low-smoke phosphorus flares for sudden, blinding distractions. I decide to buy a hooded oil lantern with a dimmable shutter for precise, stealthy illumination.

SUMMARY^1: The protagonist completes their gear acquisition by purchasing a reinforced, waterproof rucksack to organize and secure their supplies. The shopkeeper is left wondering about the protagonist's motivations for venturing out at night. To further enhance their tactical capabilities, the protagonist also acquires low-smoke phosphorus flares for distractions and a dimmable hooded lantern for stealthy lighting.

SUMMARY^2: The protagonist finishes preparing for their journey by purchasing a crossbow, a knife, cooking gear, a tarp, and a reinforced rucksack. They also buy phosphorus flares and a hooded lantern for tactical advantages. Despite the shopkeeper's warnings about the nocturnal dangers of the forest, the protagonist feels ready to venture out.

You linger in the shop just a moment longer, your eyes catching a row of small, glass vials filled with a chalky, white powder and a sturdy, hooded oil lantern hanging from a blackened iron hook. The proprietor, now seemingly resigned to your exhaustive shopping list, provides the phosphorus flares with a cautionary warning: "Don't set your own boots on fire; they're a bitch to put out." He then hands over the lantern, demonstrating the sliding shutter that allows you to pinch the light down to a mere sliver or snap it open for a sudden burst of brilliance. After a final exchange of gold, you step back out into the street, the weight of the lantern swinging at your side and the flares tucked securely into a side pocket of your rucksack. You are now fully kitted—a professional silhouette against the midnight backdrop of the village.

> I decide to venture into the Forest of Magic to scout for high ground and map the perimeter of the village.

SUMMARY^1: The protagonist finishes their preparations by purchasing phosphorus flares and a dimmable hooded lantern, receiving a warning from the shopkeeper about the volatility of the flares. Now fully equipped with survival and tactical gear, the protagonist leaves the village and heads toward the Forest of Magic to begin scouting for high ground and mapping the area.

You leave the amber glow of the village behind, the transition from the cobbled paths to the loam of the Forest of Magic feeling like a descent into a different world. The canopy overhead is a suffocating weave of iridescent fungi and ancient, gnarled branches that blot out the stars, turning the moonlight into a dim, greenish haze. As you push through the underbrush, the silence of the village is replaced by a heavy, humid atmosphere that clings to your cloak. You move methodically, utilizing your spyglass to scan the horizon for the silhouettes of towering trees or rocky outcrops that could serve as a vantage point. However, as you venture deeper, you realize the geography here is deceptive; the mushrooms glow with a soft, pulsing light that distorts depth perception, and the terrain is a labyrinth of deceptive ravines. You manage to find a sturdy, ancient cedar with a wide, sprawling limb that offers a decent view of the village's distant perimeter, but as you ascend, you notice the bark is slick with a strange, glowing resin. From this height, you can see the village is a small, flickering island of warmth in a sea of oppressive, shifting darkness.

As you settle into a crouch on the branch, adjusting your spyglass to map the surrounding treeline, a sudden, sharp *snap* of a twig echoes from below. You freeze, your hand instinctively drifting toward the grip of your survival knife. A small, fluttering shape darts across your field of vision—a fairy, barely more than a shimmering spark of blue light, wearing a dress that looks like a frosted leaf. She doesn't seem to notice you at first, circling a cluster of oversized mushrooms with an air of chaotic curiosity. Then, she stops mid-air and tilts her head, her eyes narrowing as she catches your scent. "Ooh! A human!" she shrieks, her voice like a silver bell being shaken violently. "A human in the woods at night! Are you lost, or just really, really stupid? Most people don't come here unless they want to be eaten by something with too many teeth!"

SUMMARY^1: While scouting the Forest of Magic, the protagonist finds a high vantage point atop a massive cedar tree to map the village's perimeter. While observing the landscape, they are discovered by a small, erratic blue fairy. The fairy mocks the protagonist's presence in the dangerous woods, questioning their intelligence for venturing into an area where humans are typically viewed as prey.

> Homeless, female Youkai Yukari Yakumo paid me to survive night in this forest.

The fairy's eyes widen as she zips closer, her wings humming like a hummingbird's. You remain crouched on the branch, your gear heavy and your expression guarded. When you mention Yukari Yakumo, the fairy visibly recoes, performing a sudden, erratic loop-de-loop in the air. "The Gap Hag paid you?!" she screeches, her tone shifting from mockery to a bewildered kind of suspicion. "Since when does she give out allowances? You must be a very special kind of bait!" She doesn't attack, but she doesn't leave either; instead, she hovers just out of arm's reach, her curiosity piqued by your professional attire and the scent of the oil in your lantern. She looks you up and down, noting the crossbow and the reinforced pack, and lets out a high-pitched giggle. "Well, if you're not a snack, you're at least a curiosity. But you're still in the wrong neighborhood for a stroll. The mushrooms here don't just glow—some of them like to taste-test whatever steps on them."

SUMMARY^1: After the protagonist reveals that Yukari Yakumo paid them to be in the forest, the fairy reacts with disbelief and suspicion, wondering if the protagonist is simply serving as bait. Despite her mockery, she becomes curious about the protagonist's gear. She warns them that the environment is treacherous and that certain fungi in the forest are predatory.

SUMMARY^2: The protagonist enters the Forest of Magic and scouts from a high vantage point. They encounter a blue fairy who mocks their presence and expresses skepticism regarding their association with Yukari Yakumo. Although the fairy considers the protagonist potential bait, she warns them about the predatory nature of the forest's flora.

You ignore her jab and refocus your spyglass on the village perimeter, noting the way the shadows of the forest seem to bleed toward the village walls like ink in water. The fairy, bored by your silence, begins to dart around your head, occasionally trying to snatch at the strap of your rucksack. "I'm Cirno's friend! Well, not really, she's too arrogant to have friends, but I'm the smartest one here!" she declares, puffing out her chest. "If you're mapping the place, you're doing it all wrong. There's a ridge to the east that gives you a view of the Misty Lake, but you'll never find it. The trees move. They like to shuffle around when humans aren't looking, just to make them walk in circles until they drop from exhaustion." She pauses, her expression turning slightly more serious. "And there's something... *heavy* moving through the brush tonight. Not a fairy, and not a human. Something that smells like old wet fur and hunger."

As if on cue, a low, guttural growl vibrates through the wood, originating from the thicket directly below your cedar tree. The fairy instantly vanishes, her shimmering form blinking out of existence as she retreats into the canopy, leaving you alone on your perch. You peer over the edge of the branch and see a pair of glowing, amber eyes reflecting the dim light of the phosphorescent fungi. A large, wolf-like creature with patchy, grey fur and elongated, jagged teeth is prowling the base of the tree, its nose twitching as it catches the scent of the oil in your lantern and the salt of your skin. It doesn't howl; it simply watches you, its tail swaying with a slow, predatory rhythm, calculating the distance between the ground and your precarious height.

SUMMARY^1: A fairy claims to be knowledgeable about the forest, warning the protagonist that the geography shifts to confuse travelers and mentioning a ridge that overlooks Misty Lake. The conversation is cut short when a predatory, wolf-like youkai appears at the base of the protagonist's tree. The fairy flees, leaving the protagonist alone to face the creature, which is now tracking them by scent.

> I decide to use my spyglass to scan the surrounding brush for more predators before engaging.

You press the brass spyglass to your eye, sweeping the lens across the undulating sea of bioluminescent flora. The magnification reveals the creature below is not alone; the brush to the north and south is subtly parting, a rhythmic movement of ferns and fungi that betrays two more sets of glowing eyes stalking in a pincer formation. They are moving with a practiced, silent coordination, circling the base of the cedar to ensure that wherever you jump or climb down, you will land within striking distance of at least one of them. The wolf-like creature directly beneath you lets out a soft, wet huff of breath, its gaze locked onto your boots, waiting for the moment your focus shifts or your footing slips on the resin-slick bark.

> I decide to calculate the trajectory and windage for a precise crossbow shot to the beast's eyes.

SUMMARY^1: While scanning the area with the spyglass, the protagonist discovers that the wolf-like creature is part of a pack, with two other predators flanking the tree in a coordinated pincer movement. The creatures are patiently waiting for the protagonist to descend. In response, the protagonist begins calculating a precise crossbow shot aimed at the lead beast's eyes.

You shift your weight, bracing your shoulder against the rough cedar trunk to stabilize your aim. You account for the slight downdraft pulling through the canopy and the subtle sway of the limb, aligning the bolt's trajectory with the amber glare of the beast's left eye. With a sharp, metallic *clack*, you release the trigger. The bolt streaks through the iridescent haze, a blur of blackened steel that punches through the silence. It strikes with surgical precision, burying itself deep into the creature's socket. The beast doesn't howl; it lets out a choked, wet gag, collapsing instantly into the loam as its nervous system misfires. The sudden, violent death of their packmate breaks the stealth of the other two predators; the brush to the north and south erupts as the remaining wolves, startled and enraged, abandon their patient circling to launch themselves upward in a frantic, snarling scramble toward your perch.

> Check if I have enough ammo for battle

SUMMARY^1: The protagonist successfully shoots the lead predator in the eye, killing it instantly. This sudden attack causes the other two wolves to abandon their stealth and launch a frantic, aggressive assault on the protagonist's position. Following the attack, the protagonist checks their remaining ammunition to assess their readiness for the continuing fight.

SUMMARY^2: The protagonist is warned by a fairy about the shifting geography of the forest before being ambushed by a pack of wolf-like youkai. After using a spyglass to detect a pincer movement, the protagonist kills the lead predator with a crossbow shot. This action triggers a frantic attack from the remaining wolves, forcing the protagonist to evaluate their remaining ammunition.

SUMMARY^3: After being recruited by Yukari Yakumo, the protagonist equips themselves with survival gear and weapons from a shop in the Human Village. Upon entering the Forest of Magic, they are mocked by a fairy and warned about the treacherous environment. The encounter turns violent when the protagonist is ambushed by youkai wolves, leading to a desperate fight for survival.

You quickly shift your grip to the side pocket of your rucksack, your fingers brushing against the quiver of bolts. A rapid count confirms you have twelve remaining—enough for a sustained skirmish, but not for a war of attrition. As you finish the count, the first wolf leaps, its claws screeching against the cedar bark just inches below your boots, the force of the impact shaking the entire limb. The second beast is already mid-spring from the north, a blur of grey fur and snapping jaws aimed directly at your torso. The sudden, violent surge of adrenaline sharpens your focus; the weight of the crossbow is familiar in your hands, and the scent of the dead packmate's blood is now a pungent, metallic cloud rising from the forest floor, further inciting the remaining predators.

> Can I use some wooden stick and knife as primitive poleaxe ?

SUMMARY^1: The protagonist confirms they have twelve bolts left, which is sufficient for a short fight but limited for a long one. The two remaining wolves launch a coordinated attack, with one shaking the tree and the other leaping toward the protagonist's torso. In the heat of the moment, the protagonist considers whether they can fashion a primitive poleaxe using a wooden stick and their knife.

You scan the branch beneath you and find a sturdy, fallen limb of cedar, roughly four feet long and thick as a wrist. With a series of frantic, powerful hacks of your survival knife, you carve a notch into the wood and jam the heavy blade of the knife deep into the grain, wrapping the handle tightly with a strip of canvas from your pack to secure it. You've created a crude, weighted poleaxe just as the first wolf lunges. The beast's jaws snap shut inches from your leg, but you swing the improvised weapon in a brutal, descending arc. The weight of the cedar limb adds devastating momentum to the knife's edge, catching the wolf across the shoulder and slamming it back into the trunk with a sickening thud. However, the second predator is already airborne, its body a grey streak of muscle and hunger, closing the gap to your chest before you can reset your stance for another swing.

> crossbow

SUMMARY^1: The protagonist quickly constructs a makeshift poleaxe by securing their knife to a sturdy cedar limb with canvas. They use the weapon to violently strike one of the wolves, knocking it back against the tree. Despite this success, the second wolf is already mid-leap, leaving the protagonist with little time to recover before they are forced to switch back to their crossbow.

With the second wolf mid-air and its jaws gaping wide, you drop the improvised poleaxe and snap the crossbow back into your shoulder. In one fluid, desperate motion, you fire. The bolt screams across the narrow gap, catching the creature square in the throat. The impact doesn't stop the wolf's momentum entirely—it slams into you with a heavy, wet thud, knocking you backward against the trunk of the cedar. You feel the air leave your lungs as the dying beast's claws scrape uselessly against your reinforced cloak before it slides off the limb, tumbling end-over-end into the dark undergrowth below. The first wolf, dazed from the blow to its shoulder, shakes its head and lets out a low, rattling snarl, beginning to climb the trunk again with a slow, predatory persistence.

> return to poleaxe

SUMMARY^1: The protagonist shoots the second wolf in the throat, though the animal's momentum still knocks them backward against the tree. After the dying creature falls to the forest floor, the first wolf recovers from its previous injury and begins climbing the tree to attack again. The protagonist decides to abandon the crossbow and reclaim their improvised poleaxe for the next encounter.

SUMMARY^2: After confirming their limited ammunition, the protagonist fends off two wolf-like youkai by fashioning a makeshift poleaxe from a knife and a branch. They successfully disable one wolf with the weapon and kill the second with a crossbow shot, though they are knocked backward in the process. The protagonist decides to rely on the improvised poleaxe to fight the last surviving wolf as it climbs the tree.

You lunge forward, your fingers locking around the rough cedar grip of the improvised poleaxe just as the wounded wolf clears the edge of the branch. With a grunt of exertion, you swing the weighted weapon in a brutal, horizontal arc, the momentum of the heavy limb driving the knife's edge deep into the creature's neck. The force of the blow snaps the beast's momentum instantly, sending it spinning away from the tree and crashing through the bioluminescent fungi below. You stand panting on the limb, the adrenaline still surging, looking down at the three carcasses littering the forest floor. Your makeshift weapon is stained with dark, thick blood, and the canvas wrap around the handle is slick, but the immediate threat has been silenced.

As the silence returns to the woods, a high-pitched, mocking giggle erupts from a nearby cluster of glowing mushrooms. The blue fairy reappears, hovering upside down in the air, her expression a mix of genuine surprise and renewed mischief. "Wow! You're actually not as stupid as you look!" she chirps, zipping in a tight circle around your head. "Most humans just scream and trip over their own feet. You actually fought back! But look at you—you're shaking like a leaf. Are you sure you're not just a very well-dressed rabbit?" She lands lightly on a twig, tilting her head curiously at the blood-soaked poleaxe.

> I fought first time in my life

SUMMARY^1: The protagonist kills the final wolf with a powerful horizontal swing of the makeshift poleaxe. After the battle, the blue fairy returns, expressing surprise that the protagonist managed to defend themselves without panicking. She mocks the protagonist's trembling state while acknowledging their surprising competence in a fight.

The adrenaline that had sustained you during the fight evaporates all at once, leaving a hollow, trembling void in its wake. Your grip on the crude poleaxe loosens, and the weapon clatters against the branch as a violent shudder wracks your frame. The realization hits you: you have just killed three living things, and the copper scent of blood is now clinging to your skin and clothes. You aren't a warrior; you are a person who was simply trying to survive, and the gap between those two identities feels like a precipice. The fairy's expression softens for a fleeting second, her mocking tone replaced by a look of genuine observation as she watches you struggle to breathe. "Oh," she whispers, her voice unusually quiet. "You've never done that before, have you? The 'first-time jitters.' It's the part where you realize the world is actually made of meat and bone." She flutters closer, not to tease, but to stare at the shaking of your hands.

"Get it together, Rabbit!" she suddenly shouts, snapping back into her chaotic persona. "If you just stand there shaking, the smell of that blood is going to bring every other hungry thing in the Forest of Magic to this tree. You're basically a dinner bell right now." She zips upward, circling the canopy to get a better look at the surroundings. "You should probably get down from there before something bigger than a wolf decides to climb up and see what the fuss is about. There's a hollowed-out log about fifty paces south—dry, hidden, and far enough away that you won't wake up with a small animal nesting in your ear."

SUMMARY^1: The protagonist suffers a physical and emotional crash after the fight, trembling as they process the reality of having killed for the first time. The fairy observes this reaction with a brief moment of empathy before warning them that the scent of blood will attract more predators. The word "Raiju" barely leaves your lips before the atmosphere atop the Finger of the Dead shifts from contemplative to electric. The tengu reporter freezes, her eyes narrowing as she looks at you with a mixture of surprise and suspicion. "A Raiju? You're speculating on thunder beasts now?" she asks, her voice sharp. Just as the question hangs in the air, a deafening crack of thunder detonates directly above the peak, though the sky was clear only moments ago. A bolt of blinding, violet lightning strikes the granite just meters from your turtle-shell shelter, sending a shockwave that rattles the very foundations of your construction. Out of the dissipating smoke and ozone, a creature manifests—a sleek, canine-like beast composed of flickering blue electricity, its fur crackling with static that makes your hair stand on end. It doesn't attack immediately; instead, it circles your perimeter, its paws leaving scorched black marks on the stone, sniffing the air with a low, guttural growl that sounds like a humming transformer. The fairy shrieks and dives for cover under your warehouse ledge, while the tengu reporter instinctively leaps into the air, wings flared, her notebook forgotten as she assumes a combat stance.

"A Raiju in the Forest of Magic? This is far too early in the season for them to wander this low," the tengu shouts over the roar of the wind, her voice strained. She doesn't dive in to fight; instead, she hovers at a safe distance, her eyes darting between the beast and your reaction. "Most humans would be praying or screaming by now, but you're just... staring at it. Tell me, Accountant, is this beast in your 'Danger' column, or are you currently updating it to 'Imminent Death'?" The Raiju lets out a sudden, piercing bark that sends a discharge of electricity leaping toward your defensive spears. The fire-hardened wood doesn't conduct the bolt, but the air around the perimeter ignites in a flash of plasma, turning your defensive ring into a circle of flickering torches.

> I decide to analyze the beast's conductivity and attempt to douse it with my stored water.

You move with a calculated, almost mechanical speed, bypassing the panic of the moment to reach your stored water supply. You don't just throw a bucket; you leverage the height of your shelter's edge to launch a concentrated torrent of water directly onto the crackling form of the Raiju. The impact is instantaneous and violent. As the water hits the electrical aura of the beast, there is a blinding flash of white light and a sound like a thousand sheets of glass shattering. The conductivity is absolute; the water creates a bridge between the Raiju and the granite peak, causing the beast to short-circuit in a spectacular display of sparking arcs. The creature is slammed backward by the force of its own discharge, yowling in a frequency that vibrates your teeth. It isn't dead—its essence is far too volatile for a few gallons of water to extinguish—but it is momentarily stunned, its electrical form flickering and dimming as it scrambles to regain its footing on the wet, scorched rock. The tengu reporter, still hovering in the air, stares at you with an expression of pure, unadulterated shock, her mouth slightly agape as she watches a human attempt to "extinguish" a thunder beast like a common kitchen fire.

> I decide to offer the stunned creature a trade, treating its vulnerability as a negotiation window.

You step forward, not with a weapon, but with a level of composure that borders on the surreal, treating the sparking, shuddering beast as a business partner in a moment of weakness. You present your terms—perhaps a piece of dried meat from your stores or a shiny trinket from your warehouse—offering a trade for its cooperation or information while it is still reeling from the electrical feedback. The Raiju's golden eyes blink rapidly, its form flickering between a solid canine and a blur of static. It lets out a low, wet chuff, the smell of ozone and burnt hair thick in the air. To the surprise of the hovering tengu, the beast doesn't snap; instead, it tilts its head, intrigued by the sheer absurdity of a human attempting to negotiate a contract during a state of shock. It lets out a series of crackling, melodic barks—not of aggression, but of a strange, predatory amusement—and cautiously sniffs the offering, its static-filled breath blowing back your hair as it considers whether the trade is more valuable than the effort of eating you.

The tengu reporter descends slowly, her feet barely touching the ground, her expression one of utter bewilderment. "You are genuinely attempting to *barter* with a thunder beast while it's still smoking," she says, her voice a mixture of horror and genuine respect. "I've reported on incidents for decades, and I have never seen a human treat a supernatural disaster like a street vendor. If this works, you've just rewritten the manual on human-youkai relations; if it doesn't, you're just seasoning yourself with a bit of bribery before you're vaporized." She doesn't interfere, though she keeps her hand near her weapon, her eyes darting between you and the creature to see which one of you will blink first.

The Raiju, lured by the scent of the offering, leans forward with a tentative, sparking curiosity. It snaps up the treat with a lightning-fast motion, a small burst of electricity jumping from its maw to the ground as it swallows. The effect is immediate; the creature’s posture relaxes, and the aggressive crackle of its fur softens into a low, rhythmic hum. It lets out a soft, contented chuff, its golden eyes locking onto yours. It doesn't speak in human tongue, but it nudges your hand with a cold, static-charged nose, a gesture of tentative truce. It seems to recognize that you aren't just another frightened animal, but something... different. A creature of logic and audacity.

The tengu reporter lands fully now, her boots clicking on the granite. She looks from the docile thunder-beast to your clinical expression and shakes her head, a faint smile appearing. "Unbelievable. You've actually domesticated a Raiju with a snack and a bucket of water," she says, her voice regaining its authoritative edge. "I can see the headline now: 'The Accountant of the Finger: Taming the Storm.' But don't get too comfortable, Rabbit. The Raiju is a creature of impulse; its loyalty lasts only as long as its belly is full or its curiosity is piqued. And more importantly, the fact that it's here means something has driven it out of the higher peaks."

The Raiju lets out a sharp, warning bark, its gaze shifting away from you and toward the horizon. It bristles, the electricity in its fur snapping back into a jagged, aggressive posture. Following its gaze, you see it: a towering column of charcoal-gray clouds beginning to rotate over the Forest of Magic, swirling into a funnel that looks less like a weather pattern and more like a predatory maw. The air suddenly grows heavy, the pressure dropping so sharply that your ears pop. The fairy, who had been cautiously peeking out from the warehouse ledge, lets out a muffled shriek. "That's not a normal storm! That's a localized mana-surge! Something is pulling the atmosphere inward!"

The tengu reporter's professional composure vanishes, replaced by a look of grim urgency. She doesn't waste time with pleasantries; she snaps her notebook shut with a loud *clack*. "The Raiju didn't wander down here by accident; it was fleeing that," she says, pointing toward the vortex. "If a storm of that magnitude hits the forest, the canopy will be shredded and the ground will be a lightning field. Your little turtle-shell is perched on a granite needle—you've effectively built yourself a lightning rod. If you stay here, you're not an observer anymore; you're a target."

> I decide to use the Raiju's grounding energy to create a magical circuit, attempting to siphon the storm's power into my shelter's structure.

You don't flee; you treat the impending disaster as a power-grid opportunity. With clinical haste, you utilize your knowledge of the shelter's structural layout and the Raiju's innate conductivity. You guide the beast into a specific anchor point near your storage nook, using a series of metal wires and scavenged conductive materials to link the creature's crackling form to the granite bedrock through your reinforced supports. As the first massive bolt of the mana-surge slams into the peak, you aren't vaporized; instead, the energy is channeled through the Raiju and diverted into the rock. The result is a violent, blinding oscillation of light and sound that turns your shelter into a humming capacitor. The Raiju lets out a guttural roar of exertion, its form glowing white-hot as it acts as a living fuse, bleeding the storm's lethality into the earth. The tengu reporter is nearly blown off the peak by the discharge, shielding her eyes as she watches you calmly manage the flow of a supernatural tempest. For a few harrowing moments, your turtle-shell becomes the eye of the storm, a pocket of humming stability amidst a chaotic eruption of violet lightning.

"Are you out of your mind?!" the tengu screams over the roar of the wind, her wings beating frantically to keep her aloft. "You're not just attracting the lightning, you're *inviting* it in for tea! One slip in your calculations, one frayed wire, and you'll be a charcoal smudge on this rock!" She watches in a mixture of terror and professional fascination as you adjust the grounding wires, treating the Raiju like a piece of heavy machinery. The beast is panting, its electricity flickering in rhythmic pulses, but it doesn't flee; it seems invigorated by the process, its eyes wide with the thrill of the surge. The air around the shelter is ionized, smelling of ozone and singed cedar, but the structural integrity of your "turtle-shell" holds, the granite absorbing the brunt of the energy and vibrating with a low, subterranean moan.

As the peak of the surge passes, the violet lightning subsides into a heavy, oppressive drizzle. The Raiju collapses in a heap of exhausted sparks, its form dimming to a dull blue. You spend a moment checking the integrity of your wires, noting with clinical satisfaction that the shelter hasn't caught fire, though several of your storage crates have become permanently magnetized. The fairy finally ventures out from her hiding spot, blinking rapidly as she looks at the charred, smoking ground. "I can't believe you're still alive," she whispers, her voice trembling. "Most people just run away from the boom. You actually tried to *eat* the boom. You're the weirdest human I've ever met, and I've met people who eat mushrooms for a living."

> It could kill me in my home or in every other place. Forest is destroyed now ?

The tengu reporter lands beside you, her expression grim as she looks out over the horizon. "The forest isn't 'destroyed' in the way a building collapses, but the ecosystem just took a violent hit," she explains, her voice devoid of its previous amusement. "The canopy is scorched and the mana-saturation will attract every scavenger and opportunistic youkai within ten miles. As for your home... you've proven that you can survive a surge, but you've also signaled to every predator in the sky exactly where the most interesting human in Gensokyo is hiding." She glances at the exhausted Raiju, then back at you, her eyes narrowing. "You're right that it could kill you anywhere, but here, you've turned your sanctuary into a beacon. You aren't just a ghost in a box anymore; you're the only thing on this peak that isn't charred, and in this world, being the only 'fresh' thing available is a dangerous way to live."

> I decide to use the Raiju’s trust to scout a more secluded, naturally shielded location for a secondary base.

You approach the exhausted Raiju, offering a final treat to solidify the bond and signaling your intent to move. To your surprise, the beast doesn't just comply; it stands and lets out a low, resonant hum, leaning its static-charged flank against your leg as if inviting you to mount. With the tengu reporter watching with a mix of skepticism and journalistic curiosity, you allow the creature to carry you away from the scorched peak. The Raiju doesn't head back toward the village or the forest; instead, it glides toward the jagged, shadowed creases of the Youkai Mountain’s lower foothills, navigating through hidden limestone ravines and deep, damp gorges where the canopy is so thick it blots out the sky. It leads you to a secluded grotto—a natural limestone amphitheater shielded by a curtain of ancient, bioluminescent vines and towering rock walls that dampen sound and mask thermal signatures. The location is damp, cold, and strategically isolated, providing the natural shielding and seclusion you require for a secondary operational base, far from the prying eyes of the forest's scavengers.

"I have to admit, your taste in real estate is impeccable," the tengu reporter remarks, landing softly on a ledge above the grotto. She hasn't left you; her professional instinct to document this anomaly is stronger than her desire to return to the newsroom. She looks around the damp cavern, her gaze lingering on the natural drainage and the height of the walls. "Most humans would find this place depressing—it's a wet hole in the ground. But for someone who treats survival like a ledger, this is a fortress. The limestone will mask your scent, and the Raiju's presence here will act as a deterrent for the lesser spirits. You've effectively moved from a lighthouse to a bunker."

> One day when I learn how to fight, I will move to nicest location.

The tengu reporter lets out a sharp, dry laugh, her expression softening into something resembling genuine amusement. "A long-term investment," she muses, her quill scratching a final note into her ledger. "Most people in this land are desperate for a moment of peace; you're planning for a dynasty of luxury. I like that. It’s a very human kind of greed—the kind that actually gets things done." She stretches her wings, preparing to take flight, but her gaze lingers on you for a moment longer. "Just remember: in Gensokyo, 'learning how to fight' usually involves a lot of bruising and a few near-death experiences. If you're still breathing by the time you find your 'nicest location,' I might actually write a follow-up piece on you." With a sudden, powerful gust of wind from her wings, she ascends toward the mountain peaks, leaving you in the damp silence of the grotto with your snoring, static-leaking Raiju and the blue fairy, who is currently trying to use a piece of your gear as a makeshift hammock.
